Give readable names to clusters

Source: R/name_clusters.R
name_clusters.Rd

A cluster identifier ("01", "cl_12") says nothing about its content. name_clusters() gives each cluster a provisional label that helps reading plots and tables, with one of four methods: the words that distinguish the cluster from the others ("tf-idf"), the metadata of its most central node ("tidygraph_functions") or of its node with the highest value of a given column ("given_column"), or a label written by a language model from a description of the cluster ("llm", optional, through the ellmer package: a model on your computer or an online service). These labels are starting points for interpretation, not the result of it: naming a cluster requires reading its documents, the references they share, and what distinguishes them from neighbouring clusters (Ding 2011) .

Usage

name_clusters(
  graphs,
  method = c("tidygraph_functions", "given_column", "tf-idf", "llm"),
  name_dynamic_clusters = FALSE,
  cluster_id,
  label_columns,
  label_name = "cluster_label",
  tidygraph_function = NULL,
  order_by = NULL,
  text_columns = NULL,
  nb_terms_label = 3,
  prompt_columns = NULL,
  nb_nodes = NULL,
  llm = NULL,
  instructions = NULL,
  context = NULL,
  preview = FALSE,
  name_merged_clusters = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

graphs

A tbl_graph or a list of tbl_graphs.

method

"tf-idf" (chosen when no method is given), "tidygraph_functions", "given_column" or "llm" (see the details).

name_dynamic_clusters

Logical. TRUE when cluster_id identifies clusters across a list of graphs (the dynamic clusters of merge_dynamic_clusters()): each cluster then gets one name, computed on all its nodes in all windows. FALSE (default) names the clusters of each graph separately.

cluster_id

Character scalar, the node column with the clusters to name.

label_columns

For "tidygraph_functions" and "given_column", the node column(s) used to build the label of the chosen node, joined by "_" (e.g. c("source_author", "source_year")).

label_name

Character scalar, the name of the new column ("cluster_label" by default).

tidygraph_function

For "tidygraph_functions", a call to a centrality function of tidygraph, such as tidygraph::centrality_pagerank() (see tidygraph::centrality).

order_by

Character scalar, a numeric node column used to rank the nodes of each cluster, for two methods (ignored by the others):

  • "given_column": the node with the highest value names the cluster, e.g. "node_size" from build_network() with compute_size = TRUE (the most cited document of the cluster);

  • "llm" (required): the nb_nodes nodes with the highest values are shown to the model, e.g. "within_module_degree" from add_node_roles() (the nodes most tied to their own cluster). For dynamic clusters, a node present in several windows is ranked by its highest value.

text_columns

For "tf-idf", the node column(s) with text (titles, abstracts, keywords), passed to extract_tfidf().

nb_terms_label

For "tf-idf", the number of terms in each label (3 by default), separated by commas. A term that is part of a term already in the label, or contains one, is skipped ("business" after "business cycle").

prompt_columns

For "llm" (required), character vector, the node column(s) written in the description of each cluster sent to the model: what the model knows about the nodes (e.g. c("source_title", "source_year", "cluster_label")). A column with one value per cluster (a label computed before, e.g. with method = "tf-idf") is given once for the cluster.

nb_nodes

For "llm" (required), whole number, the number of nodes listed for each cluster, highest order_by first. 0 lists none: the model then reads only the context and the columns with one value per cluster.

llm

For "llm", the model: a chat object of ellmer, configured as you would for any other use, e.g. ellmer::chat_ollama(model = "mistral", params = ellmer::params(temperature = 0, seed = 123)) (see the details). Not needed with preview = TRUE.

instructions

For "llm", character scalar, the system prompt sent before the description of each cluster. NULL (default) uses the instructions given in the details. Change them to ask for longer labels, another language, another vocabulary... To start from the default, get it with preview = TRUE (column instructions), e.g. instructions = paste(prompts$instructions[1], "Answer in French.").

context

For "llm", optional character scalar describing the network to the model: what the nodes are, the field, the period, the question (e.g. "Economics articles on stagflation, 1970-2010, linked by their shared references"), written at the top of each description. Strongly recommended: in our tests on three corpora and three local models, it raised the quality of the labels more than any other change to the description (see the details).

preview

For "llm", logical. If TRUE, returns what the model would receive, without calling it (no model needed): a tibble with one row per cluster, its identifier, the instructions (the system prompt) and the description of the cluster (the user message), plus a graph column for a list of graphs named separately. Print a description with cat(). FALSE (default) names the clusters.

name_merged_clusters

Former name of name_dynamic_clusters.

...

For "tf-idf", other arguments of extract_tfidf() (e.g. clean_word_method, n_gram, ngrams_filter). Must be empty for the other methods (a misspelt argument is an error).

Value

The same object as graphs, with a new node column label_name, also joined to the edges through their cluster column. With method = "llm" and preview = TRUE, a tibble of the messages that would be sent to the model (see preview).

Details

tf-idf. Each cluster is treated as one document made of the texts of its nodes, and each term \(t\) (word or n-gram) gets the weight $$\mathrm{tf}_{tc} \times \mathrm{idf}_t = \frac{n_{tc}}{\sum_u n_{uc}} \times \log\frac{C}{\mathrm{df}_t}$$ (Spärck Jones 1972; Salton and Buckley 1988) , with \(n_{tc}\) the number of occurrences of \(t\) in cluster \(c\), \(C\) the number of clusters and \(\mathrm{df}_t\) the number of clusters where \(t\) appears. The label gathers the terms with the highest weight: frequent in the cluster, rare in the others. With name_dynamic_clusters = FALSE, the comparison is made within each graph, so clusters of different windows may get the same label.

Most central node. "tidygraph_functions" computes the centrality given in tidygraph_function on each graph (it is added as a node column) and labels each cluster with the node with the highest value. The centrality is computed on the whole graph, not within the cluster. This method needs a network structure and therefore cannot be used with name_dynamic_clusters = TRUE.

Given column. "given_column" labels each cluster with its node with the highest order_by value: for an article network, typically its most cited article.

Language model. "llm" writes a description of each cluster and asks the model given in llm for a label. The model is a chat object of the ellmer package (only needed for this method), so any model ellmer reaches can be used:

  • a model running on your computer, so that the content of the nodes stays on it: ellmer::chat_ollama() (Ollama), chat_lmstudio(), chat_vllm(), or chat_openai_compatible() for another local server (e.g. llama.cpp);

  • an online service (chat_openai(), chat_anthropic()...): the descriptions of the clusters are then sent to it.

Configure the chat object as for any other use of ellmer; for more stable labels, set params = ellmer::params(temperature = 0, seed = 123) (this does not guarantee the same labels on another computer, and some online services ignore seed). Each cluster is sent alone to a copy of llm (its earlier conversation is not sent), with instructions as the system prompt, and the answer is constrained to one label (chat_structured()). The label is cleaned: no quotes or final period, words separated by spaces ("Asset_Pricing" becomes "Asset Pricing"). The default instructions are:

`r llm_default_instructions`

Writing the prompt. We compared nine prompts, with three local models (gemma3:4b, gemma3:12b, qwen3:14b) on 21 clusters of three corpora (articles of economics), the labels being scored blind by another model (accuracy and specificity, from 1 to 5; a small test, to be taken as an indication). What mattered most, in order:

  1. The instructions. Short ones ("a label of 2 or 3 words") give generic labels ("Monetary policy analysis"); the default above, which asks for the specific topic, forbids empty words and gives examples, raised the scores by 0.5 to 0.8 points whatever the model.

  2. The context: one sentence on what the nodes are, the field and the period raised the scores by a further 0.25 to 0.5 points. It helps the model most where it cannot tell the cluster apart by itself.

  3. Little else: 10 nodes are enough (25 did not help, 5 was a bit worse); year and journal in prompt_columns changed little; and a column of key terms (tf-idf) did not help and produced more repeated labels. A larger model did not systematically beat a small one once the prompt was good. If you change instructions, keep the rules asking for a specific topic and keep the context.

With ellmer::chat_ollama(), a model that thinks before answering (e.g. qwen3) can take minutes per cluster or time out, because ellmer reaches Ollama through its OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where think = FALSE is ignored: use api_args = list(reasoning_effort = "none").

The description of a cluster gathers, when available:

  • the context you give;

  • the number of nodes of the cluster (and of windows, for dynamic clusters);

  • the columns of prompt_columns with one value per cluster (e.g. a tf-idf label computed before with method = "tf-idf"), given once;

  • its nb_nodes main nodes (highest order_by), described by the other columns of prompt_columns.

Everything comes from the node tables of graphs. The value of a node longer than 300 characters (an abstract) is cut, and its line breaks are removed; columns with one value per cluster are written in full. Use preview = TRUE to read the descriptions before running the model.

If the model fails on the first cluster, name_clusters() stops: the problem is likely its configuration (try llm$chat("Hello")). A later cluster whose label fails is labelled "no_name" with a warning. By default, each answer may take up to 300 seconds, with up to 3 tries (the options ellmer_timeout_s and ellmer_max_tries of ellmer): raise options(ellmer_timeout_s = ) for a slow model. A warning is given when a description exceeds about 4000 tokens: some local servers cut longer prompts without warning (Ollama has a context of 4096 tokens by default).

Nodes of an unnamed cluster get "no_name".

References

Ding Y (2011). “Community Detection: Topological vs. Topical.” Journal of Informetrics, 5(4), 498–514. doi:10.1016/j.joi.2011.02.006 .

Salton G, Buckley C (1988). “Term-Weighting Approaches in Automatic Text Retrieval.” Information Processing & Management, 24(5), 513–523.

Spärck Jones K (1972). “A Statistical Interpretation of Term Specificity and Its Application in Retrieval.” Journal of Documentation, 28(1), 11–21.

See also

extract_tfidf() to see more terms than the labels show.

Examples

network <- build_network(
  nodes = subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation"),
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  method = "similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1
)
#> ℹ Coupling (`biblionetwork::biblio_coupling()`) with "similarity": ties
#>   weighted by the idf-weighted cosine of the two lists of targets, after Shen
#>   et al. (2019), between source_id entities sharing target_id entities.
#> ℹ Two source_id are linked when they share at least 1 target_id
#>   (`edges_threshold`).
#> ℹ Nodes without any edge are removed (`keep_singleton = FALSE`).
network <- add_clusters(
  network,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  seed = 123,
  verbose = FALSE
)

# The words of the titles that distinguish each cluster
network <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "tf-idf",
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  text_columns = "source_title",
  nb_terms_label = 3,
  clean_word_method = "none"
)

# The article with the highest PageRank of each cluster
network <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "tidygraph_functions",
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  label_columns = c("source_author", "source_year"),
  label_name = "central_article",
  tidygraph_function = tidygraph::centrality_pagerank()
)
unique(tidygraph::as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")[
  c("cluster_leiden", "cluster_label", "central_article")
])
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   cluster_leiden cluster_label                            central_article
#>   <chr>          <chr>                                    <chr>          
#> 1 02             great inflation, stabilization, monetary VELDE-F_2004   
#> 2 01             productivity, unemployment, prices       WACHTER-M_1978 
#> 3 04             stagflation, inflation, 1970s            DELONG-B_1997  
#> 4 03             oil, great stagflation, price shocks     BARSKY-R_2002  

# What a language model would read for each cluster (no model needed):
# titles, years and the tf-idf label, for the 10 nodes most tied to their
# own cluster
network <- add_node_roles(network, cluster_id = "cluster_leiden")
prompts <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "llm",
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  prompt_columns = c("source_title", "source_year", "cluster_label"),
  order_by = "within_module_degree",
  nb_nodes = 10,
  context = "Economics articles on stagflation, linked by their shared references.",
  preview = TRUE
)
cat(prompts$instructions[1])
#> You label the clusters of a network for a researcher.
#> A cluster is a group of nodes (e.g. documents) more linked to each other than to the rest of the network.
#> You receive the description of one cluster, with its most central nodes.
#> 
#> Rules:
#> - Name the topic the nodes share, in 2 to 4 words of ordinary language, e.g. "Protein folding", "Urban heat islands", "Medieval trade routes".
#> - Be as specific as the information allows: prefer "Coral bleaching" to "Marine biology". Avoid empty words (studies, analysis, issues, research) and the name of a whole field when the nodes share a narrower topic.
#> - Base the label on what most nodes have in common, not on one odd node; if the topics are mixed, name the dominant one.
#> - Use only the information given.
#> - Answer with the label alone: no quotes, no final period.
cat(prompts$description[1])
#> Context of the network: Economics articles on stagflation, linked by their shared references.
#> 
#> Cluster "01": 69 nodes.
#> cluster_label: productivity, unemployment, prices
#> 
#> Main nodes (highest within_module_degree first; source_title | source_year):
#> - ENERGY PRICE INCREASES AND MACROECONOMIC POLICY | 1980
#> - THE VARIANCE AND ACCELERATION OF INFLATION IN THE 1970S: ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATORY MODELS AND METHODS | 1980
#> - MACRO POLICY RESPONSES TO PRICE SHOCKS | 1979
#> - INFLATION, FLEXIBLE EXCHANGE RATES, AND THE NATURAL RATE OF UNEMPLOYMENT | 1981
#> - THE REAL PRICE OF OIL AND THE 1970S WORLD INFLATION | 1981
#> - THE INFLATIONARY IMPACT OF HIGHER ENERGY PRICES 1973-1975 | 1978
#> - INFLATION IN THEORY AND PRACTICE | 1980
#> - INSTITUTIONAL FACTORS IN DOMESTIC INFLATION | 1978
#> - THE 1971-1974 CONTROLS PROGRAM AND THE PRICE LEVEL: AN ECONOMETRIC POST-MORTEM | 1981
#> - COMMENT ON <93>THE ACCELERATION OF INFLATION<94> | 1979

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# A label written by a model running on your computer, here with Ollama
# (install Ollama, then `ollama pull mistral` in a terminal)
network <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "llm",
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  prompt_columns = c("source_title", "source_year", "cluster_label"),
  order_by = "within_module_degree",
  nb_nodes = 10,
  label_name = "llm_label",
  llm = ellmer::chat_ollama(model = "mistral",
                            params = ellmer::params(temperature = 0, seed = 123)),
  context = "Economics articles on stagflation, linked by their shared references."
)
} # }
